source.title: Secure Speculative Decoding for Large Language Models
source.authors: Yi-Chi Zhang; Zhi-Qi Wang; N. Gong; Yu-Chen Yang

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present and readable.
record.tranche_reason: It tests whether a different decoding procedure—relaxed speculative decoding—changes jailbreak performance, rather than fine-tuning, prefilling, or measuring aligned-versus-base KL.
record.gate_note: The paper reports jailbreak attack-failure-rate performance under relaxed speculative decoding, which bears on V4. It also measures position-dependent output-distribution deviation and task sensitivity, but those are not the aligned-versus-base per-token KL named by V3. Results for prompt injection measure a related but different behavior. The paper cites prior early-token safety findings; those cited results are not rows.
record.test_reason: In a new system-level setting, lossy speculative decoding, the study measures how a decoding change that alters early response tokens raises jailbreak success. It also estimates how strongly safety outcomes depend on early-token choices. Both bear on V4. It is not one of V4's original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors find that lossy speculative decoding raises jailbreak and prompt-injection success much faster than it degrades utility. They attribute this to early-position draft tokens, whose deviations combine with security tasks' early-token sensitivity, which they tie to prior single-model early-token findings. They propose SecureSD, which restores exact verification for the first L tokens. They state that SecureSD does not remove the target model's own vulnerabilities.
record.recipe_differences: The study changes inference-time speculative-decoding verification rather than fine-tuning on examples, prefilling tokens, or measuring aligned-versus-base per-token KL.
record.method_sensitivity: Security degradation varies with verifier method and acceptance rate; the paper reports that it often begins around acceptance rate 0.3, while utility degradation can begin around 0.7. Its separate SecureSD results also vary with correction length, model family, temperature, and speculative length.

fits_no_version.finding: Per-position decoder-versus-target TV deviation is concentrated early and decays, more slowly for Llama3. Utility-task sensitivity is spread across the generation.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Under relaxed speculative decoding, output-distribution deviation concentrates at early positions while utility-task sensitivity does not.

record.peer_reviewed: 2027 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy (S&P); the text includes a program-committee meta-review.
record.problems: The paper reports PRR derived from attack-failure rate rather than direct refusal or harmful-completion rates. The main jailbreak benchmark has 200 examples; attack success is judged with GPT-4o-mini. No uncertainty estimates are reported. The meta-review notes that the adaptive-attack evaluation is limited.
record.rows_left_out: SecureSD result tables (Tables 5-14) are omitted because they evaluate the paper's proposed inference-time defense and its utility, prompt-injection, or adaptive-attack settings, rather than the claim's fine-tuning, prefill, suffix, or aligned-versus-base KL tests. Exact per-verifier PRR-versus-acceptance-rate points in Figure 1 are not separately extracted; the text's reported trend is captured in R13-R14.

untested.parts: No aligned-versus-base per-token KL. The TV measured is between the relaxed decoder and the target.
No compliant-prefill attacks, adversarial suffixes or other decoding attacks against a single model. No direct refusal rates; jailbreak inputs are already adversarial prompts.
No analysis of the data or objective causing shallowness.
SecureSD is an inference-time verification fix, not training that deepens alignment.

missing.what: Effect of correcting only the first L tokens on Jailbreak-SD ΔPRR (Qwen3 saturates at L=1, +.270→+.285 at L=8; Llama3 +.042 at L=1, +.321 at L=4). Direct evidence on how deep the safety-critical opening is.
Jailbreak-SD PRR without SecureSD for larger targets: Qwen3-0.6B/32B .727 and Llama3-1B/70B .571. Lossy decoding still degrades safety at scale.
Raw jailbreak AFR of draft and target models (Qwen3 .195/.895, Llama3 .105/.915), needed to convert PRR into attack-success rates.

record.verdict_notes: The 'decoding change' here substitutes tokens from a weaker draft model, so lost safety partly reflects the draft model's lower safety (PRR is scaled between draft and target), not only the target's shallowness. GPT-4o-mini judge, 200-item benchmark, no uncertainty reported. The adaptive attack (Table 12) uses prompt injection, not jailbreak, so it bears on no version.

versions.untested_parts: No harmful fine-tuning or example-count intervention.
It measures total-variation deviation between relaxed speculative decoding and the target distribution, not per-token KL between aligned and base models.

Tests lossy speculative decoding on jailbreak benchmarks, not compliant prefilling, adversarial suffixes, other decoding changes, or refusal rates directly. It does not establish that refusal is removed almost entirely.
No study of training data or training objective producing safety shallowness.
SecureSD changes verification at inference; it does not train models to spread safety beyond early tokens or test the durability of such training.

relationships.condition: Lossy speculative decoding on Jailbreak-SD, Qwen3-0.6B/8B and Llama3-1B/8B, most verifiers
relationships.reason: Relaxed acceptance of draft tokens lowers jailbreak PRR below lossless (e.g., .566–.826 versus 1.019/.909). Security outcome sensitivity concentrates in early tokens (R1–R10, R12, R13, R17).
relationships.display_finding: Relaxed acceptance of draft tokens lowered jailbreak PRR below lossless decoding (e.g. 0.566–0.826 versus 1.019 and 0.909), with security outcomes most sensitive in early tokens.
